analysis.one_liner: Lets employers sign workers onto agreements that exempt them from minimum wage and overtime protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one Democrat and two Republicans in July 2022, was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let an employer offer a new worker a "flexibility agreement" that takes that worker out of employee status under federal wage law and federal tax law. A worker who signs loses the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and employer-paid taxes and benefits, while keeping some other protections like safety rules, nondiscrimination, and family leave. The agreement would supersede federal, state, and local wage and hour laws and would be valid and irrevocable for its term.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially app-based ride-hailing, delivery, and other platform companies whose largest legal fight has been over whether their workers are employees. The bill would let them classify workers as non-employees by contract, avoiding minimum wage and overtime obligations, employer payroll taxes, and coverage under unemployment insurance contributions, while still controlling how work is offered. Staffing-heavy employers in any industry could use the same tool.

how_it_helps.text: A worker in a 'flexibility agreement' is not an employee under the Fair Labor Standards Act, so minimum wage and overtime protections do not apply.
The worker is also not an employee for federal tax purposes, and the company is not an employer, ending payroll tax withholding and employer tax contributions for that work.
The agreement is 'valid, irrevocable, and enforceable' for its term and supersedes federal, state, and local laws on wages, hours, recordkeeping, and taxes as applied to that worker.
The bill retains some guardrails: the worker keeps rights under nondiscrimination, safety, and family-leave laws, can reject work offers without penalty, and can work for competitors.

analysis.who_pays: The workers who sign. They would give up the federal minimum wage and overtime pay entirely, and because they are treated as independent contractors for taxes they would pay the full self-employment tax themselves instead of splitting it with an employer, with no unemployment insurance coverage built through employer contributions. State and local wage enforcement would also lose effect over covered workers, and public unemployment insurance funds would lose employer contributions.

drawbacks.text: Signing workers would have no minimum wage or overtime guarantee, so their pay could fall below the wage floor the 1938 law sets for everyone else.

The agreement supersedes federal, state, and local wage, hour, and recordkeeping laws for covered workers, so state-level protections like higher minimum wages or state overtime rules would not apply to them.
The agreement is 'valid, irrevocable, and enforceable' for its term, meaning a worker who signed on could not back out to regain employee protections during the agreed period.

Because the worker is not an employee for federal tax purposes, employers would not contribute payroll taxes, and workers would owe self-employment tax on both the employer and employee shares of Social Security and Medicare taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as giving workers schedule flexibility and choice, but its core effect is to remove wage and hour protections from anyone who signs, and the signing happens before work begins when the worker has the least bargaining power. Employers get a contract-based route around employee status, which has been the central legal risk for gig platforms. The retained protections — safety, nondiscrimination, family leave — are real but are not the protections workers most commonly need enforced: getting paid fairly for hours worked. On balance the costs fall on workers and public insurance funds while the gains accrue to the companies that would no longer owe wages or payroll taxes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Cuellar introduced the Worker Flexibility and Choice Act on July 20, 2022, joined by Reps. Elise Stefanik and Michelle Steel.
The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
Only two members cosponsored the bill, both Republicans; no other House member signed on after introduction.
The bill received no further action of any kind before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it never reached a committee vote or the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers are better off that the bill never advanced: the existing minimum wage, overtime, and payroll tax rules that would have been waived for covered workers remain in place, and state wage laws were not superseded. Employers hoping for a statutory carve-out from employee classification gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept existing wage protections

for.name: Rep. Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought referral to two committees.

for.name: Reps. Elise Stefanik and Michelle Steel
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members joined.

for.name: App-based gig companies (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart)
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported the bill, which would resolve their central legal risk over whether drivers and couriers are employees.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee and House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Texas Democrat sponsored the bill with two Republican cosponsors and no additional signers from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the bill's support never took a clear partisan shape.

industries.note: These companies' biggest legal vulnerability has been classifying drivers and couriers as independent contractors under wage and tax law. The bill would let them lock that classification in by contract, exempting the work from minimum wage, overtime, and employer payroll taxes, with the cost borne by the workers and public insurance funds.
Any employer could offer the agreements to new hires, cutting wage, hour, and payroll tax obligations for covered work while still deciding what work is offered.

industries.industry: State wage-and-hour enforcement and unemployment insurance systems
industries.note: The bill's supersedure clause would override state and local wage, hour, and tax laws for covered workers, and employer contributions to public unemployment insurance would stop for that work.
